system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

Chapter 5: 3-PART 4THS

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 5 — 3-PART 4THS

_Pages 9-10._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## diminished 4th enharmonic problem

> The problems involve the interval of a diminished 4th. To be more specific, we're talk-
>
> ing about B and Eb. A diminished 4th looks like a 4th on the staff. But the sound is a Major 3rd.

**Significance (p. 9).** Defines the core enharmonic trap that makes some 3-part 4th voicings sound like triads.

## voicings fail quartal context

> That is not to say that there is anything wrong with these voicings. It’s just that they
> don’t work very well in a 4th voicings context.

**Significance (p. 9).** Practical rule for when to avoid certain voicings in quartal context.

## tertial vs quartal harmony

> Triads are 3-part chords based on tertial harmony (harmony derived from 3rds). 3-part
> 4ths are 3-part chords based on quartal harmony (harmony derived from 4ths). As it turns out,
> tertial harmony and quartal harmony are pretty much exact opposites.

**Significance (p. 9).** Conceptual definition that frames the entire system.

## triad interval totals

> Four 3rds, Two 4ths, One 5th, Two 6ths
> Primary intervals: 3rds and 6ths
> Secondary intervals: 4ths and 5ths
> Color intervals: 2nds and 7ths (missing)

**Significance (p. 10).** Interval taxonomy of triads — comparative baseline.

## 4th voicing interval totals

> Two 2nds, Four 4ths, Two 5ths, One 7th
> Primary intervals: 4ths and 5ths
> Secondary intervals: 2nds and 7ths
> Color intervals: 3rds and 6ths (missing)

**Significance (p. 10).** Interval taxonomy of 3-part 4ths — mirror-image proof of tertial/quartal opposition.

## drop-D pedal technique

> Here's a really great thing to do that is very “guitar-friendly.” After you've spent some
> time exploring the 3-part 4ths in C Major, tune the low E string down a whole step to D. Use
> the low D string as a pedal, [you could also use the A string] and play through all the cycles!

**Significance (p. 10).** Concrete guitar-specific drop-D pedal technique for 4th-voicing cycles.

## D Dorian no avoid notes

> you’d be playing in D dorian mode; since there
> aren’t any “avoid” notes in Dorian, pretty much anything and everything you play will work
> very nicely!

**Significance (p. 10).** Explains why drop-D Dorian pedal context is safe to explore freely.

## arpeggiating for melody

> you might also consider the possibility of ARPEGGLIATING
> the 4th voicings to arrive at WAY COOL melodies!

**Significance (p. 10).** Extends 4th voicings from harmonic to melodic generation.
